extracted.intended_audience: reporters and newspaper journalists (prospective and practicing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing leads and bodies for news stories (interviews, speeches, courts, fires, accidents, and crime), including how to feature elements, handle quotations, and structure lists and continuing reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of Interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In a story containing a number of interviews, let the lead feature the consensus of opinion expressed in the interviews. Then follow in the body with the individual quotations, each man's name being placed prominently at the beginning of the paragraph containing his interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is a large number of interviews, the name may even be set in display type at the beginning of the paragraph. If the persons interviewed are not prominent but their statements are worthwhile, the quotations may be given successively and the names buried within the paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads for Speeches (options)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter may begin a speech story by featuring: (i) the speaker's theme; (2) the title of the address; (3) a sentence or paragraph of forceful direct quotation; (4) an indirect quotation of one or more dynamic statements; (5) the speaker's name; (6) the occasion of the speech; or (7) the time or the place of delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any one of these may be played up according to its importance in the address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring a Single Sentence (quotation lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quotation of a single sentence or a single paragraph is happiest if one can be found that will give the keynote of the speech or will harmonize with a declared policy of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a sentence/paragraph that gives the keynote; examples in the text illustrate effective single-sentence quotation leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random Statements as Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis should be laid on the value of playing up in the lead even a random statement if it chances to agree with a specific policy or campaign to which the paper has committed itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are valuable because they appear unprejudiced; conversely, ignore such statements if opposed to the paper's views. Always make clear the precise relation of the featured quotation to the speech as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Quotation in Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief reason for quoting indirectly in the lead a single statement of a speaker is the need of shifting an important point to the very first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect quotation to place an important idea first; ensure the indirect rendering conveys the speaker's real meaning and spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title Featured
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the subject (title) of the speech as a feature is advisable when it is particularly happy or when it expresses the theme of the address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature the title when it clearly signals the address's theme or is notably apt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Featured
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme may be featured when a single-sentence quotation cannot readily be found and the subject does not indicate the nature of the address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the theme to summarize the core idea when other single-sentence options are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Lead (speeches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long summarizing leads of speeches are to be avoided as a rule, since they are liable to become overloaded and cumbersome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a summarizing lead, keep individual clauses relatively short and simple and make their relation to each other and the whole absolutely clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's Name Featured
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker's name comes first only when he is sufficiently prominent locally or nationally to justify featuring him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature the name first for highly prominent speakers; otherwise choose other lead devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring the Occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Featuring the occasion of a speech or the auspices under which it was given is justifiable only when the speech and the speaker are of minor importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the occasion as the hook when speaker/subject are not primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring Time and Place
rubrics_metrics.description: Only rarely is the time or the place featured. But either may be played up when sufficiently important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature time/place only when they materially affect the story or are of unusual interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring Several Details (long lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the speaker, the subject, the occasion, and the place are all important, it may be needful to make a long summarizing lead of several paragraphs, explaining all these features in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to use a quarter- or half-column before getting to the address itself when multiple elements are important (example: presidential campaign speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body Coherence with Lead (speech stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing the body of the story, the first thing to strive for is proper coherence with the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lead uses a quotation from the middle of the speech, follow it with a paragraph of development, then proceed with quoted material which may not follow the speaker's original order; avoid incongruity between an epigrammatic lead and the succeeding quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in Quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Only what one has taken down verbatim should be put within quotation marks. All else should be reported indirectly with an unwavering determination to convey the real spirit of the lecture or sermon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put paraphrase or reconstructed paragraphs in quotes; quotation marks assert exact wording and misuse can lead to misunderstandings and denials by speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech Story as a Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The story as a whole should be a little speech in itself. Whole topics may be omitted; others may be cut down to a single sentence; still others may be presented in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert quotation marks and cohering phrases (e.g., 'said he', 'continued the speaker') carefully to clarify what is direct quotation vs condensation; vary connecting phrases and liven the report with gestures, facial expressions, and eccentricities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of Speeches (coverage strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting a series of speeches, it generally is the best policy to play up at length the strongest address or the speech of the most important personage, then summarize the remaining talks in a paragraph or so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all speeches are of equal importance, feature the general trend of thought or a single startling statement; give each speaker space according to the value of his address and place the speaker's name first in the paragraph where he is quoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banquets, Conventions, etc. (alternate features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not always are speeches important, or even delivered, on these social, political, and holiday occasions. If not, the reporter must devote his attention to the occasion, to any unusual incidents or events, or to the persons attending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reporting banquets focus can be persons present, novelty of favors, originality of menu; in conventions, purpose, expected results, effects on legislation, or new ideas; in trade conventions find features in incoming styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current Magazine/Article News Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories of articles appearing in current magazines, books, government publications, educational journals, and the like are of the same type as stories of addresses. The lead may feature the theme, the title, the author, a single sentence, an entire paragraph, the society publishing the article, or the motive back of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Body usually follows with direct quotations summarizing the whole. Avoid extended analysis or learned comment; report only details of interest to readers, not to instruct the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court Stories as Interview+Speech Combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Court, trial, and inquest stories are but a combination of the methods of handling interviews and speeches: the questions and answers being the interviews, the arguments and decisions being the speeches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead varies by stage: if verdict, feature guilt/innocence/penalty/rehearing; if intermediate, feature cause, significant testimony, important witness, point reached, probable length, clashes over testimony, or prisoner's attitude; body may include quotations from testimony and arguments, with summarizing paragraphs of evidence and proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation Practices in Court Reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally it may become necessary to quote verbatim questions and answers in cross-examination, but generally a more readable story may be had by reporting the testimony continuously and omitting the questions altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote verbatim only when essential to bring out significant points in depositions; otherwise paraphrase testimony for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting Legal Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when playing up a court decision, it is rarely wise to quote large extracts verbatim, owing to the heaviness of legal expression and the frequent use of technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when the form of the decision as well as the facts is vital should the language of the decree be quoted at length. Better to print the entire decision separately and write an independent summarizing story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing Trials (contextual connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing up trials continued from preceding days, one must be careful to connect the story with what has gone before, explaining who the persons are, the cause of their appearance in court, and where the trial is being conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient background so readers who have not followed prior reports can understand the present story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous Court Stories and Libel Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: A word of caution against the temptation to write court stories humorously at the expense of accuracy and the feelings of those drawn into public notice. Libel lurks in wrong street numbers, misspelled names, misplaced words and phrases, and accidental resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not warp facts to make a good story; report truthfully — a journalist loses credibility the moment the paper is wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident and Crime Story Grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident and crime stories are grouped together because they are handled alike; they differ in point of view (criminal act vs misfortune), and often overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods like those for fires as a type for accident stories generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead to a Fire Story (who/what/when/where/why/how/how_much)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily the lead to a story of a fire should tell what was destroyed, the location of the property, the extent of the damage, the occupants or owners, the time, the cause, and what made the loss possible — answering who, what, when, where, why, how, and how much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack the lead with the key facts; example shows property destroyed, location, owner, loss amount and insurance status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lives Lost or Endangered (priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of, or danger to, life, unless other features are exceptional, should take precedence over every other particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature fatalities or life-endangering details above property or other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists of Killed or Wounded (format rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing a story where a number of persons have been killed or injured, the reporter should: 1. Separate the names of the dead from those of the injured, putting the list of dead first. 2. Record the names in alphabetical order, placing surnames first. 3. Put each name, with the age, address, occupation, nature and extent of the injury, and any care given, in a separate paragraph. 4. Underscore the names with wave lines so that they shall be printed in display type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this exact ordering and paragraphing to aid readability and typesetting; example layout provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of Heroism (feature worthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of heroism involving danger to or loss of life are always good for features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize heroic acts in leads or features to heighten interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remarkable Escapes (feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarkable escapes from burning buildings, in their appeal to the elemental struggle for life, make valuable features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe escapes vividly; they provide strong human-interest hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous, Pathetic, or Daring Incidents (feature selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous, pathetic, or daring incidents are worth featuring strongly, particularly when they involve children, aged persons, or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select humanizing or emotionally resonant incidents to enliven fire/accident stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of Fire (feature if unusual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of the fire, if unusual or mysterious, may be featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature unusual causes (e.g., Santa Claus whiskers and a candle) to give the story an angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings or Property as Features
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular buildings, if especially valuable by reason of their age, location, or cost of construction, may be features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight historic, architecturally notable, or economically significant properties when they are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Fire Features (occupants, insurance, response)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may feature any of a number of particulars: occupants of the building, the owners, prominent persons involved, the amount and character of the damage, the amount of insurance, how the fire was discovered, how it spread, when the alarm was given, the promptness or delay of the fire department, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature any of these particulars provided it has unusual importance or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the Fire Story (details to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: Somewhere in the story the extent of the damage and the amount of insurance should be given. Greater emphasis can be given by quoting direct statements of eye-witnesses or of persons injured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include damage extent and insurance; use eyewitness accounts (janitor's account, survivor recollections) to add interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rumors at Fires (verification caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reporting a fire, particularly a big one, the reporter should guard against the wild rumors about the extent of the loss, the number of persons injured or burned to death, the certainty of arson, etc., which usually gain currency among the spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never take such stories at face value; investigate until details are accurate, or omit them or record them as mere rumors. Keep calm to judge information's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident Stories in General (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident stories in general follow the same constructive plans as those given for fires. The lead should play up the number of lives lost or endangered, the cause of the accident, the extent of the damage or injury, the time, and the place, answering who, what, when, where, why, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many killed or hurt and names obtainable, make lists as directed; then continue the body in simple chronological order, reserving other details as appropriate.
